hooks.text: The Big Dipper’s stars are drifting apart in opposite directions.
The Big Dipper is actually a cosmic illusion falling apart.
Seven stars are currently breaking the Big Dipper apart.

title: Why the Big Dipper is breaking apart
description: The iconic spoon of the night sky is actually a group of stellar strangers drifting in different directions.

beats.text: The Big Dipper’s stars are drifting apart in opposite directions.
beats.visual: photograph of the Big Dipper asterism in a dark night sky

beats.text: We usually see this spoon as a permanent cosmic landmark.
beats.visual: star map showing the Ursa Major constellation with the Big Dipper outlined

beats.text: Astronomer Richard Proctor found a secret drifting family in 1869.
beats.visual: portrait of British astronomer Richard Anthony Proctor

beats.text: Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, and Mizar are stellar siblings.
beats.visual: diagram of the Big Dipper with the five central stars glowing brighter

beats.text: They're all traveling together toward the constellation Sagittarius.
beats.visual: telescope view of a rich star field in the constellation Sagittarius

beats.text: But the stars at the ends are total strangers.
beats.visual: diagram of the Big Dipper with the two end stars highlighted in a different color

beats.text: Dubhe and Alkaid are actually zooming the other way.
beats.visual: proper motion diagram with arrows showing stars moving in opposite directions

beats.text: This tug-of-war will bend the handle until the spoon dissolves in 100,000 years.
beats.visual: time-lapse animation showing the Big Dipper shape distorting over time

beats.text: The famous spoon is slowly breaking into pieces.
beats.visual: wide field image of the night sky where the Dipper stars are scattered

better_than_last: Used the myth_vs_fact structure to clarify the internal motion of the Big Dipper and applied the authority rule by centering the discovery on Richard Proctor.
